title: Singapore Airlines Deepens Role at Air India as Losses Cross $3 Billion
excerpt: The Southeast Asian carrier is placing executives in key operational roles at India's flag carrier as the Tata Group-led turnaround proves far more costly and complex than anticipated.
body:
• Singapore Airlines has moved executives into Air India's flight operations, engineering, and maintenance functions, escalating from strategic partner to hands-on operational presence.
  • Air India posted an estimated net deficit of $3 billion in the financial year ending March 2026, worsening from $2.4 billion the prior year.
  • SIA CEO Goh Choon Phong and Tata Group Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran have met to discuss a funding road map and the search for a new CEO after Campbell Wilson's resignation.

Singapore Airlines is taking a far more active role inside Air India, deploying its own executives into critical operational positions as India's flag carrier battles record financial losses, safety lapses, and the departure of its chief executive.

SIA has placed its people in key roles across flight operations, engineering, and maintenance at Air India in recent months — areas where the Singaporean carrier has long been considered a global benchmark, according to people familiar with the matter.

A Turnaround Under Strain

The deeper involvement marks a notable escalation since a deadly Boeing 787 Dreamliner crash in June 2025 that killed more than 240 passengers and plunged Air India into its worst crisis. What began as a strategic partnership has evolved into a far more hands-on presence, with SIA now effectively running core operational functions while the Tata Group — which owns 74.9 percent of Air India — focuses on commercial, human resources, finance, and IT.

Air India reportedly approached Tata Sons and Singapore Airlines for at least $1.14 billion (INR 10,000 crore) in additional funding after posting losses of $2.4 billion in the financial year ending March 2025. Losses worsened further in the year ending March 2026, with the carrier posting an estimated net deficit of approximately $3 billion.

"We have been working closely with our partner Tata Sons to support Air India's transformation programme."

— Singapore Airlines spokesperson

SIA's Own Bottom Line at Stake

The urgency is not one-sided. Singapore Airlines reported that Air India was largely responsible for a 57.4 percent year-on-year drop in the group's net profit to SGD 1.2 billion ($921 million). Losses from associated companies, primarily Air India, reached SGD 178 million ($139 million) in the December 2025 quarter alone. The airline has said it remains "firmly committed" to supporting Air India's transformation but has conceded that the lack of visibility on when Air India can turn a profit is a growing concern.

SIA CEO Goh Choon Phong has described the turnaround as a "long game" with no "shortcuts," while declining to comment on possible future capital injections.

Operational Challenges Mount

Beyond finances, Air India faces a cascade of operational problems. European regulators have flagged compliance issues. Aircraft were reportedly flown without valid airworthiness certificates. The June 2025 crash forced the airline to cut services and triggered closer scrutiny of its engineering practices.

Geopolitical disruptions have compounded the difficulties. The closure of Pakistani airspace to Indian overflights and conflicts in the Middle East have forced longer, more expensive routing at a time of elevated jet fuel prices. To stem losses, Air India plans to cancel 27 percent of its international flights — nearly 150 weekly services — between June and August 2026.

To bolster operations, Singapore Airlines has seconded Basil Kwauk as chief operations officer and Jeremy Yew as head of engineering and maintenance at Air India.

Leadership Vacuum

Adding to the complexity, CEO Campbell Wilson announced his resignation, leaving the carrier searching for new leadership at a critical juncture. Goh and Tata Group Chairman Natarajan Chandrasekaran met in Mumbai to discuss both a funding road map and the CEO search, the Economic Times reported.

Wilson, a veteran Singapore Airlines executive who had been seconded to lead Air India's transformation, oversaw the ambitious merger with Vistara — the Tata-SIA joint venture — in 2024. SIA invested INR 3,194.5 crore to secure its 25.1 percent stake in the expanded entity.

What Comes Next

The Tata Group acquired Air India from the Indian government in 2022 with a vision to restore the carrier to its former stature. More than four years on, that goal remains distant. The airline is burning through cash, cutting routes, and relying increasingly on its minority shareholder for operational expertise.

For the Indian diaspora community, many of whom depend on Air India for long-haul routes connecting India with North America, Europe, and Southeast Asia, the airline's struggles carry direct consequences. Route cuts between June and August 2026 are expected to reduce capacity on key diaspora corridors during the peak summer travel season.

Whether the additional funding materializes — and in what form — will likely determine the pace of Air India's turnaround in the months ahead.
